title: Reforms to super bad for business
full_text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers was warned by his own department that the government’s payday superannuation reforms could see small businesses hit with fines – even if they pay employee super on time – if funds fail to process payments before weekly deadlines.
Payday Super laws passed parliament in 2025, with the rules coming into effect in July this year.
But new internal documents released under freedom of information show Treasury warned Dr Chalmers that small and medium enterprise could be slapped unfairly.
The warning flagged that “employers (were) being exposed to SG charge (penalties) where there are delays in contributions being successfully received and allocated, despite them paying the amount on time initially”.
To address the issue, Treasury officials said it would be a “key focus of the non-legislative elements of the measure”, meaning it wasn’t accounted for in the legislative reform.
Treasury told Dr Chalmers it would rely on the ATO revising the system to ensure transactions are processed swiftly.
The Treasurer was also warned that industry stakeholders, across Australia and globally, flagged they would need an 18-month lead time to “secure funding and effect the changes” following the legislative reforms. But the business sector got 10 months’ notice from when the bill was introduced to parliament until the changes came into effect.
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry CEO Andrew McKellar said only 50 per cent of businesses were prepared for the change to payday superannuation.
“Payday super is hitting (the) cashflow of small business, right when they need some breathing room, it should have been delayed,” Mr McKellar said. “No small business should be hit with a fine for doing the right thing and we need assurances that will not occur.” He said the ACCI had urged the government to delay the changes until next year, but its pleas were ignored.
Shadow treasury spokesman Tim Wilson said that “like the warnings that his spending would fuel inflation, interest rates and debt, Jim Chalmers hasn’t listened to warnings about the risks of ramming through payday super rules”. A Treasury spokesman said the reforms “include important changes that ensure there are more tailored and proportionate consequences where superannuation contributions are not received on time, replacing the punitive consequences for minor delays that may have occurred under the old law”.
